  %\VignetteIndexEntry{Power and sample size for C-QTc analyses with cqtcpower}

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4)
library(cqtcpower)
```

In a parallel single ascending dose (SAD) study, the concentration-QTc (C-QTc)
analysis concludes that a drug has **no clinically relevant QT effect** when the
upper bound of the one-sided 95% confidence interval of the predicted
$\Delta\Delta QTc$ at the supratherapeutic concentration $C_{supra}$ is below
$U_0 = 10$ ms. `cqtcpower` tells you how likely that conclusion is (power) and
how many subjects per cohort you need (sample size).

## 1. Describe the study

Concentrations come either from a one-compartment PK model or from a fixed
profile.

```{r design}
des <- cqtc_design(
  conc = conc_pk_1cmt(dose = c(1, 3, 10, 30, 100, 200, 400, 800),
                      Ka = 0.8, CL = 12000, V = 40000, iiv_sd = 0.1),
  n_active = 6, n_placebo = 2,
  times = c(1, 2, 4, 8, 12, 16, 24)
)
des
conc_typical(des)$true_cmax   # helps choose C_supra
```

## 2. State the truth you plan for

`U1` is the true $\Delta\Delta QTc$ at `C_supra`. `theta_Z` is a
concentration-independent treatment effect. `slope_cv` sets between-subject
variability of the C-QTc slope (or give `sigma1` directly).

```{r params}
par <- cqtc_params(U1 = 5, C_supra = 0.008, theta_Z = 0.5,
                   sigma_e = 5, sigma0 = 8, slope_cv = 0.75)
par
```

## 3. Power

```{r power}
cqtc_power(des, par)
```

`RI` and `RS0` estimate $\theta_C C_{supra}$ only; `RI + Z` and `RS0 + Z` also
estimate the treatment effect, which costs power but protects against a
concentration-independent drug effect.

Power across cohort sizes:

```{r curve}
pc <- cqtc_power_curve(des, par, n_per_cohort = seq(4, 40, by = 4))
plot(pc)
```

## 4. Sample size

```{r ss}
cqtc_sample_size(des, par, power = 0.8)
```

The cohort size moves in blocks that keep the 6:2 active:placebo ratio (4, 8,
12, ...).

## 5. Check by simulation

`cqtc_simulate()` simulates studies, fits the mixed models with `lmerTest`, and
reports empirical power, coverage and bias next to the analytical power. It is
also the only way to evaluate the correlated random-slope models `RS` and
`RS + Z`. Each replicate fits every requested model, so start small:

```{r sim}
sim <- cqtc_simulate(des, par, nsim = 30, models = c("RI + Z", "RS0 + Z", "RS + Z"),
                     ddf = "Wald")
sim
```

For a real check use `nsim = 1000` or more, Kenward-Roger degrees of freedom
(`ddf = "Kenward-Roger"`, needs the `pbkrtest` package), and run in parallel:

```{r parallel, eval = FALSE}
future::plan("multisession", workers = 8)
sim <- cqtc_simulate(des, par, nsim = 1000, ddf = "Kenward-Roger", parallel = TRUE)
```

Simulation-based sample size (for example for `RS + Z`) starts at the
analytical answer and steps block by block:

```{r sim-ss, eval = FALSE}
cqtc_sample_size(des, par, models = "RS + Z", method = "simulation",
                 nsim = 500, ddf = "Kenward-Roger", parallel = TRUE)
```

## Notes on the analytical approximation

The closed-form covariance of $(\hat\theta_Z, \hat\theta_C)$ assumes known
variance components and that treatment and concentrations are uncorrelated with
baseline QTc. For random-slope models it additionally approximates the
fixed-effect block of the information matrix by its random-intercept form. In
the settings of the accompanying paper the resulting standard error of
$\hat U$ is within about 3% of the exact GLS value.
